name: Driving while intoxicated with child passenger (ordinary state jail felony)
officialTitle: DRIVING WHILE INTOXICATED WITH CHILD PASSENGER.
conduct: Operating a motor vehicle in a public place while intoxicated when that vehicle is occupied by a passenger younger than 15. The statute does not require a crash or injury, parenthood, or proof that the passenger is the driver’s child. A passenger aged 15 does not meet this age condition. This ordinary profile does not assume either §49.09(b) qualifying-prior finding. Section 49.09(d)/(g) governs final convictions, specified deferred adjudication and the prohibition on using the same conviction for both this enhancement and Chapter 12 enhancement. Historical or foreign predicates require their own exact verification; this choice does not establish that any particular prior qualifies. Intoxication can mean loss of normal mental or physical faculties from the listed substances or a statutory alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more; a 0.08 test is not indispensable under the faculties theory. Lawful entitlement to use a substance is not a defense under §49.10. Section 49.11 removes the need to prove a separate culpable mental state; it does not remove the conduct, intoxication or causation elements.
penalty: State jail felony: ordinarily 180 days to two years in a state jail and a possible fine up to $10,000. The ordinary §49.04 Class B, open-container or 0.15 profiles do not replace this separate child-passenger offense. For qualifying motor-vehicle intoxication convictions, Transportation Code §709.001 adds its traffic fine ($3,000, $4,500 or $6,000 under its distinct conviction-period/test conditions); a judicial indigency finding requires waiver of fines and costs under that section. Separate license, community-supervision and case-specific consequences require review. Qualifying priors and other legally required findings can change punishment.

name: Intoxication assault (ordinary serious bodily injury)
conduct: By accident or mistake, causing serious bodily injury to another by reason of intoxication while operating an aircraft, watercraft or amusement ride, or while operating a motor vehicle in a public place; alternatively, causing that injury as a result of assembling a mobile amusement ride while intoxicated. The public-place condition attaches to the motor-vehicle alternative, not automatically to every listed mode. Section 49.07(b) requires substantial risk of death, serious permanent disfigurement, or protracted loss or impairment of a bodily member or organ; ordinary bodily injury alone is insufficient. Intoxication must cause the injury under the statutory alternative, not merely coincide with an accident. This ordinary profile excludes the special victim/duty and traumatic-brain-injury findings in §49.09(b-1)/(b-4). Intoxication can mean loss of normal mental or physical faculties from the listed substances or a statutory alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more; a 0.08 test is not indispensable under the faculties theory. Lawful entitlement to use a substance is not a defense under §49.10. Section 49.11 removes the need to prove a separate culpable mental state; it does not remove the conduct, intoxication or causation elements.

name: Intoxication Manslaughter
conduct: Operating a motor vehicle in a public place, an aircraft, watercraft or amusement ride, or assembling a mobile amusement ride, while intoxicated, and by reason of that intoxication causing another’s death by accident or mistake. The public-place requirement attaches to motor-vehicle operation. Being intoxicated when someone dies does not alone establish the required causal link. The two retained 2025 versions of §49.09(b-2) share the protected-victim grade; one additionally addresses multiple deaths and the other a prior intoxication conviction plus a Chapter 51 violation. That Chapter 51-dependent branch is not cleared by this choice and requires separate predicate, version and applicable enforcement verification; it is not declared invalid or inapplicable. Intoxication can mean loss of normal mental or physical faculties from the listed substances or a statutory alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more; a 0.08 test is not indispensable under the faculties theory. Lawful entitlement to use a substance is not a defense under §49.10. Section 49.11 removes the need to prove a separate culpable mental state; it does not remove the conduct, intoxication or causation elements.
penalty: Second-degree felony: ordinarily two to 20 years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. This is the ordinary second-degree range, not a claim that every §49.08 case has that grade: qualifying protected-victim or multiple-death findings can produce first-degree punishment (five to 99 years or life and up to $10,000). For multiple §49.07/49.08 convictions arising from one criminal episode, §3.03(b)(1) permits concurrent or consecutive sentences; this is not an automatic stacking requirement.  For qualifying motor-vehicle intoxication convictions, Transportation Code §709.001 adds its traffic fine ($3,000, $4,500 or $6,000 under its distinct conviction-period/test conditions); a judicial indigency finding requires waiver of fines and costs under that section. Separate license, community-supervision and case-specific consequences require review. Qualifying priors and other legally required findings can change punishment. If community supervision is granted, article 42A.401 requires at least 120 days of confinement for this conviction/enhancement; this does not promise supervision eligibility. For applicable offenses from September 1, 2023, article 42.0375 requires court-set monthly restitution for a child whose parent or guardian was the victim, through age 18 or high-school graduation, whichever is later, but not once the recipient is 19. The court determines the reasonable necessary amount using the statutory factors; confinement does not automatically erase arrears.
